corrected_value.authors: Dumontheil, I., Apperly, I. A., & Blakemore, S. J.
corrected_value.title: Online usage of theory of mind continues to develop in late adolescence.

decisions.quote:
The current study had three main objectives: (a) to replicate the behavioral findings of Dumontheil
and colleagues (2010), (b) to assess the role of inhibitory control in this task across age groups, and (c)
to compare the time course of information processing among children, adolescents, and adults
through eye-tracking in order to determine in what ways the deployment of ToM differs across age
groups.
decisions.location: Discussion, p. 14, lines 727-731 (reference entry at p. 17, lines 921-922)
decisions.reason: The primary study explicitly states that its first main objective is to replicate the behavioral findings of Dumontheil, Apperly, & Blakemore (2010) ('Online usage of theory of mind continues to develop in late adolescence', Developmental Science, 13, 331-338; no DOI printed in the text). The shipped row's outcome_quote is from this paper's Abstract describing the Director task replication of Dumontheil et al. (2010), but the shipped citation metadata (Cacchione & Call, 2010, 'Intuitions about gravity and solidity in great apes: the tubes task', 10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00881.x) is a metadata mislink to a different article in the same 2010 volume of Developmental Science that is never cited in the paper. The blind coding (target 0) correctly identifies Dumontheil et al. (2010).

decisions.quote:
To summarize, children and adolescents made more errors than adults only in the Director Exper-
imental trials, which required taking the perspective of the director into account, in contrast to the
rule-based control condition (No-Director Experimental trials). This replicated the behavioral results
reported in Dumontheil and colleagues (2010).

Reaction time. Analysis of RT showed that children responded more slowly than the adolescents and
adults in all trial types except for the Director Experimental trials, which showed no difference among
age groups (see supplementary material for analyses). These results are also in line with those
reported in Dumontheil and colleagues (2010).
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Dumontheil, Apperly, & Blakemore (2010), the authors state an explicit overall replication verdict that their behavioral results replicated Dumontheil et al. (2010): children and adolescents made significantly more errors than adults in Director Experimental trials but did not differ in No-Director Experimental trials, and reaction times did not differ across age groups in Director Experimental trials. The inhibitory control (Go-NoGo) and eye-tracking analyses were novel extensions rather than failures of the original. Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'successful'.

decisions.reason: The study collected new behavioral and eye-tracking data from a fresh sample of 65 participants (children, adolescents, and adults) to re-test the published behavioral findings of Dumontheil, Apperly, & Blakemore (2010) on the computerized Director task. Both shipped and blind codings agree that the record type is 'replication'.
